prior_decision.quote: Numerous developmental studies of predominantly urban Western middle-class children suggest that children reach this milestone by 18 to 24 months of age. By 18 months, approximately 50% pass and by 24 months a significant majority of children (more than 70%) are reported to self- refer by touching or removing a mark from their own body (face or other body region) while exploring their mirror image (Amsterdam, 1972; Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière, 1996; Bard, Todd, Bernier, Love, & Leavens, 2006; Bertenthal & Fisher, 1978; Lewis & Brooks-Gunn, 1979; Lewis & Ramsay, 2004; Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima, 2003; Schulman & Kaplowitz, 1976). Here we report cross-cultural observations on the emergence of mirror self-recognition (MSR), using a simplified mark test, raising questions regarding the meaning and universal validity of this test as an ontogenetic benchmark of self-concept.
prior_decision.reason: Bertenthal and Fisher (1978) is attributed not only in the introduction's 18-to-24-month Western benchmark set that the paper attempts to replicate across cultures, but also in the Method and General Discussion sections as a direct source of the >60% (60% to 85%) pass-rate benchmark tested via the binomial analysis and contrasted with the cross-cultural results. Rejecting it in favor of Amsterdam (1972) confuses Amsterdam's role as the original paradigm source with the empirical benchmark findings directly re-tested here.
